messages:
maria: Quick brain dump — we need to pick an approach for control plane tenancy that handles QoS, cost attribution, and backpressure without doubling ops work. Two options: per-tenant CP slices (strong isolation) vs shared CP with tenant-scoped priorities and quotas. Thoughts?
ben: +1 to discussing. main concerns: observability correlation across slices, and burst isolation for noisy tenants.
oliver: Isolation is nice but per-tenant slices -> much higher infra overhead and slower rollout for CP changes. Also harder to maintain global routing policies.
lei: Shared CP could use tenant-scoped tokens + priority queues. We can surface per-tenant latency SLOs in the console. But noisy tenants could still affect global controlplane latency unless we implement strict CPU/circuit breakers.
maria: Right — operational cost is huge with slices. But risk: a bad tenant bringing down shared CP affects all customers. Can we reduce blast radius without full slices?
ben: What about hybrid: lightweight logical slices (namespaces) with per-namespace resource budgets enforced at the runtime (cgroup-like quotas) + async backpressure to tenant proxies? Less infra churn than full slices.
oliver: That feels promising. Implementation notes: we'd need per-namespace metrics pipes for billing and QA. Also need a way to pin high-priority tenant traffic to reserved workers during bursts.
lei: Pinning implies routing policy changes. Proposal: keep shared CP pool, introduce a fast-path reserved pool for tenants with reserved commitments. Routing policy: if tenant_usage > reserved_threshold -> failover to reserved pool or shed non-critical work.
oncall-bot: deploy-notify: canary build cp-quota-enforcer v0.3 rolled out to 10% of CP nodes.
maria: Good. Edge cases: what about cross-tenant correlated requests — e.g., many small tenants causing a global spike? Quota per tenant helps but total headroom still finite. Need graceful degradation policy (favor SLA-paying tenants).
ben: Agree. We should define degradation tiers: 1) reserved pool for committed tenants, 2) best-effort for free tenants, 3) shed batch/low-priority ops. Also expose a "throttle_reason" in traces for easier debugging.
oliver: On billing/observability: we must emit per-request tenant_id + cost_estimate (tokens, CPU-ms) to metrics pipeline. That allows accurate chargebacks without separate slices.
lei: Implementation checklist:
- quota-enforcer sidecar in CP nodes (cgroups or tokenc bucket)
- priority-routing table (tenant -> reserved_pool boolean)
- metrics tag enrichment (tenant_id, priority, cp_node_id)
- fallback behavior: routed to reserved_pool OR return 429 with retry-after
- rollout plan: canary, monitor tail latency & error rates
maria: Rollout concerns: config surface explosion. Need a simple defaults-first policy and a small set of opt-ins for reserved pools. Start with: reserved pool only for 3 highest commit customers.
ben: SRE/infra impact: reserved pool increases capacity planning complexity. We should amortize by sharing reserved nodes across tenants with complementary peak patterns.
oliver: Also add a gate: feature flag to enable per-tenant quota enforcement globally. We can rollback quickly if we see unexpected error budgets.
lei: One more: data residency. If a tenant opts for private deployment later, we need to make sure controlplane tokens and metrics streams can be forwarded or scrubbed. Design the token format with pluggable telemetry hooks.
maria: Next steps: I can write a short RFC appendix that sketches hybrid design, controlplane-side quota enforcer API, and rollout checklist. Assign reviewers: @ben @oliver @lei. Any objections?
ben: LGTM.
oliver: LGTM, add a short test plan for surge scenarios (hundreds of small tenants ramping).
lei: I'll draft the metrics and tracing spec.
oncall-bot: reminder: please tag any changes to cp-router in the weekly deploy schedule.
